claims.text: An active-learning-trained machine-learning potential can accurately predict solid and liquid free energies and associated fusion properties.
The MLP can replace full AIMD sampling even in systems with strong anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling.
The MLP will be trained incrementally on a sparse set of ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations from both solid and liquid states.
Training on solid and liquid configurations will capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and fingerprints of electron–vibration coupling.
The trained MLP can be used for fast molecular-dynamics or Monte Carlo sampling to compute free energies near the melting point.
The intended operating temperature range is approximately 0.8–1.2 times the melting temperature.
The MLP acts as a surrogate that interpolates the ab initio free-energy landscape.
Interpolation by the MLP retains the structural and vibrational details needed for an accurate thermodynamic description.
Selective sampling and active updating of the training set enable the MLP to capture anharmonic vibrational modes relevant to phase free-energy differences.
Selective sampling and active updating enable the MLP to capture electron–vibration interactions relevant to phase free-energy differences.
Similar neural-network-potential frameworks have demonstrated high accuracy in elemental and binary systems.
Similar neural-network-potential frameworks have required much less computational expense than full AIMD in elemental and binary systems.
The approach will reduce computational cost by one to three orders of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD workflows.
MLP free energies and derived latent heats and transition temperatures will remain within approximately 5–10% of reference values.
The MLP approach will scale more favorably than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit AIMD free-energy workflows are accurate but computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD is especially computationally expensive for multicomponent systems.
The method is immediately applicable to elemental and binary systems in the range 0.8–1.2 times their melting temperatures.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy systems may fail if training data do not cover the relevant interactions and anharmonic configurational space.
An MLP free-energy deviation greater than approximately 10% across key temperatures would falsify the proposed replacement of AIMD at retained accuracy.
